pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-01.title: Split by the number of o's
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-01.body:
The letters available are $c,m,b$ once each and $o$ twice.

- **Two o's:** choose the position of the third letter ($3$ ways) and the third letter ($3$ choices: $c,m,b$): $3\cdot3=9$ words.
- **At most one o:** arrange 3 of the 4 distinct letters $c,o,m,b$: $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ words.

Total $9+24=33$.

**Answer: 33**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-01.title: Complement
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-01.body:
Words with all letters different use $3$ of the $4$ distinct letters $c,o,m,b$ in order: $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$. The only other possibility is a word with two o's: $\binom32\cdot3=9$. So $24+9=33$.

**Answer: 33**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-02.title: Work backwards
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-02.body:
Ending with $4$ coins: the last entry is $7$ from $8$ coins, or $9$ from $9$ coins (an entry of $8$ would need $1$ coin, but at least $8$ coins are needed to put in $8$). So before the last entry he has $8$ or $9$.

Going back one more entry (not repeating the same amount): to have $8$ coins he came from $12$ (put in $7$) or $13$ (put in $9$); to have $9$ he came from $13$ (put in $7$) or $14$ (put in $9$). So two entries before the end he has $12$, $13$ or $14$.

One more step back: $12$ comes from $16,9,17$; $13$ from $17,10,18$; $14$ from $18,11,19$. The start $15$ is not among $\{8,9,12,13,14\}$ or $\{9,10,11,16,17,18,19\}$, so $1$, $2$ or $3$ entries are impossible.

One forward entry from $15$ gives $10$ (put in $9$), $11$ (put in $7$) or $18$ (put in $8$), all in that last set, so $4$ entries work, e.g. $8,9,7,9$: $15\to18\to13\to9\to4$.

**Answer: 4**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-03.title: Count paths and subtract bad ones
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-03.body:
The price rises by $7$ net in $13$ days, so it goes up $10$ days and down $3$ days: $\binom{13}{3}=286$ sequences. Remove those that hit $\$0$.

To hit $0$ from $2$ the stock must first go down twice net. Paths that touch $0$: by the reflection principle, reflect the part of the path before the first visit to $0$; these correspond to paths from $-2$ to $9$ in $13$ steps, which need $12$ ups and $1$ down: $\binom{13}{1}=13$.

$286-13=273$.

**Answer: 273**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-03.title: Direct subtraction
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-03.body:
Bad sequences: down, down at the start and then one more down anywhere among the other $11$ days: $11$ sequences; or the path goes $2,1,2,1,0$ or $2,3,2,1,0$ (one extra up first) and then the rest are all ups: $2$ sequences. That is $13$ bad sequences, so $286-13=273$.

**Answer: 273**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-04.title: Linearity of expectation
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-04.body:
For one particular color, the probability it is never picked in $4$ draws is $\left(\frac9{10}\right)^4=\frac{6561}{10000}$, so it appears with probability $\frac{3439}{10000}$. By linearity, the expected number of distinct colors is $10\cdot\frac{3439}{10000}=\frac{3439}{1000}$. This is in lowest terms ($3439=19\cdot181$), so $p+q=3439+1000=4439$.

**Answer: 4439**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-05.title: Linearity of expectation
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-05.body:
The number of index pairs $(i,j)$ with $i-j>155$ is $\binom{2015-155}{2}=\binom{1860}{2}=1728870$.

For any fixed such pair, $(a_i,a_j)$ is equally likely to be any ordered pair of distinct values in $\{1,\dots,2015\}$, so the probability that $a_i-a_j>266$ is
$$\frac{\binom{2015-266}{2}}{2015\cdot2014}=\frac{\binom{1749}{2}}{2015\cdot 2014}=\frac{759}{2015}.$$
Hence the expected count is $1728870\cdot\frac{759}{2015}=651222$.

**Answer: 651222**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-06.title: Average each digit
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-06.body:
The first three digits form a $3$-subset of $\{1,\dots,9\}$ and the last three form a multiset of size $3$ from $\{1,\dots,9\}$ chosen independently. The average of the number is the sum of the average digit times place value.

**First block** $a_1<a_2<a_3$: by symmetry $d\mapsto10-d$, $\bar a_2=5$ and $\bar a_1+\bar a_3=10$. The number of triples with $a_1=k$ is $\binom{9-k}2$, so $\bar a_1=\frac{\sum_k k\binom{9-k}{2}}{\binom93}=\frac{\binom{10}{4}}{\binom93}=\frac52$, hence $\bar a_3=\frac{15}2$.

**Second block** $a_4\ge a_5\ge a_6$: again $\bar a_5=5$ and $\bar a_4+\bar a_6=10$. The number with $a_6=k$ is $\binom{9-k+2}{2}$, so $\bar a_6=\frac{\sum k\binom{11-k}2}{\binom{11}3}=\frac{\binom{12}4}{\binom{11}3}=3$, hence $\bar a_4=7$.

The average is
$$\tfrac52\cdot10^5+5\cdot10^4+\tfrac{15}2\cdot10^3+7\cdot10^2+5\cdot10+3=250000+50000+7500+700+50+3=308253.$$

**Answer: 308253**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-06.title: Direct enumeration
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-06.body:
There are $\binom93=84$ choices for the first block and $\binom{11}3=165$ for the last, so $13860$ interesting numbers. Summing all of them by computer and dividing by $13860$ also gives $308253$.

**Answer: 308253**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-07.title: Slice into layers
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-07.body:
Cut the cube into three $1\times3\times3$ layers. In each layer the $3$ rows and $3$ columns are among the $3\times1\times1$ blocks, so each layer needs at least $3$ black cubes, and exactly $3$ only when they form a permutation pattern (one in every row and column); otherwise it needs at least $4$. With $10$ cubes the layers have $3,3,4$ black cubes.

The $9$ blocks running through all three layers must also be hit, so every one of the $9$ positions in a layer must be black in some layer. Call the two layers with $3$ cubes $P$ and $Q$ (permutation patterns, $6$ each) and the third layer $R$ (4 cubes). The $6$ permutation patterns split into $3$ even and $3$ odd ones.

- **$P,Q$ of the same parity, different:** $2$ choices for $Q$ given $P$, and the two patterns are disjoint. The uncovered $3$ positions are the third pattern of that parity, which $R$ must contain, plus one more cube anywhere in the other $6$ cells: $6$ ways. Count: $3\cdot6\cdot2\cdot6=216$, where $3$ is the choice of which layer is $R$.
- **$P,Q$ of opposite parity:** $3$ choices for $Q$; they overlap in exactly one cell, so $5$ positions are covered and $R$ must contain the other $4$ exactly: $3\cdot6\cdot3=54$.
- Identical $P=Q$ cover only $3$ positions, which would need $6$ cubes in $R$: impossible.

Total $216+54=270$ (confirmed by a computer count over all $\binom{27}{10}$ choices).

**Answer: 270**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-08.title: Split into 2-by-2 blocks
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-08.body:
Two black cells in the same $2\times2$ block would touch, so each of the $9$ blocks of the $6\times6$ grid holds at most one black cell, hence exactly one. In each block the black cell is at one of four positions (left/right, top/bottom).

Left/right: if a block is "right" then the block to its right must also be "right" (otherwise the cells touch), so in each row of blocks the pattern is L...LR...R: $4$ choices per row of blocks, and similarly each column of blocks is T...TB...B: $4$ choices per column. This gives $4^3\cdot4^3=4096$ placements.

Still, black cells in diagonally adjacent blocks can touch at a corner. Using inclusion-exclusion on the $4$ interior corners (each bad corner: $2\cdot(1\cdot2\cdot4)^2=128$ placements, total $512$, with $16$ overcounted for the pairs of opposite corners), the valid count is $4096-512+16=3600$.

**Answer: 3600**

pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-08.title: Computer check
pumac-2015-combinatorics-b-08.body:
A backtracking count of placements of $9$ non-attacking kings on a $6\times6$ board gives $3600$.

**Answer: 3600**
